days.title: CI/CD Pipeline Components and Branching Strategy Fundamentals

concepts.heading: The Four-Stage CI/CD Pipeline
concepts.body: A modern CI/CD pipeline is typically composed of four sequential stages: Source (a commit in CodeCommit, GitHub, or Bitbucket triggers the pipeline), Build (CodeBuild compiles code and runs unit tests), Test (further validation such as integration tests), and Deploy (CodeDeploy pushes the validated artifact to targets). AWS CodePipeline is the orchestration layer that wires these stages together, tracking artifacts as they move from one stage to the next and enforcing that a stage only starts once the previous stage succeeds. Understanding which AWS service owns which stage is one of the most frequently tested associations on the exam.

concepts.heading: Trunk-Based Development vs GitFlow
concepts.body: Trunk-based development has developers merge short-lived feature branches into a single main branch multiple times a day, which keeps the codebase continuously integrable and is the branching model most compatible with automated CI/CD pipelines. GitFlow, by contrast, maintains long-lived release, develop, and hotfix branches, which slows down integration and suits teams needing strict release gating rather than continuous delivery. A scenario describing frequent small merges and fast feedback points to trunk-based development; a common trap is assuming more branches always means more safety, when long-lived branches actually increase merge conflict risk and integration lag.

concepts.heading: Stages, Actions, and Manual Approval
concepts.body: Within CodePipeline, a stage executes only after the prior stage completes, but the actions inside a single stage can run in parallel, for example running unit tests and a static analysis scan side by side before continuing. A Manual Approval action can be inserted between stages to force a human sign-off, commonly used before a production deployment stage, and the pipeline pauses until someone approves or rejects it through the console, CLI, or an SNS-notified link. This is the standard mechanism for implementing a deployment gate without building custom tooling; forgetting that approval actions block the whole stage, not just one action, is a frequent point of confusion.

concepts.heading: Pipeline Triggers
concepts.body: A pipeline can start automatically when its configured source changes, using either polling or, more efficiently, an event-based trigger such as a webhook from GitHub or a CodeCommit change event delivered through EventBridge. A custom EventBridge rule can also trigger a pipeline based on other conditions, such as a schedule, an S3 upload, or an event from a different pipeline. Event-based triggers are strongly preferred over polling because they reduce latency between a commit and pipeline execution and avoid unnecessary API calls; the exam often frames 'reduce delay between commit and build' as pointing to this switch.

concepts.heading: Artifacts Between Stages
concepts.body: As a pipeline runs, each stage typically produces an output artifact (for example, a packaged Lambda deployment zip) that is stored, by default, in an S3 bucket created for the pipeline. Downstream stages declare that artifact as an input so CodePipeline automatically passes the correct file set from build to deploy without custom wiring. Because these artifacts are S3 objects, they can be encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key and versioned. A key gotcha: if a custom KMS key is used, both the pipeline's role and any cross-account roles must have explicit key permissions or the deployment fails.

examPoints: When a question describes short-lived branches merged into main multiple times per day with an emphasis on fast integration, the expected answer is trunk-based development rather than GitFlow or a long-lived release branch model.

When a question requires a human to explicitly approve a deployment before it proceeds to a production stage, the expected answer is a CodePipeline Manual Approval action, not an external ticketing system or a CloudWatch alarm.

quiz.q: An engineering team wants every commit to a shared main branch to trigger an automated build and test cycle, and wants to minimize the time branches stay open before merging. Which branching strategy should the team adopt?
choices: Trunk-based development with short-lived feature branches
A single branch with no pull requests at all
quiz.explain: Trunk-based development merges small changes into main frequently, which is what continuous integration requires; GitFlow's long-lived branches would delay integration and increase merge risk.

quiz.q: A DevOps engineer must ensure that no deployment to the production stage of a CodePipeline proceeds until a release manager explicitly signs off. What should the engineer add to the pipeline?
choices: A CloudWatch alarm on the production stage
A Manual Approval action placed before the production deploy stage
quiz.explain: A Manual Approval action pauses the pipeline until a human approves or rejects it; a CloudWatch alarm monitors metrics but cannot gate a pipeline stage on human sign-off.

days.recap: Day 1 covered the four-stage anatomy of a CI/CD pipeline, why trunk-based development suits continuous integration, how Manual Approval actions gate deployments, and how event-driven triggers and S3-backed artifacts move work through CodePipeline.

days.title: Deployment Strategies Deep Dive: Blue/Green, Canary, and Linear

concepts.heading: In-Place vs Blue/Green on EC2
concepts.body: CodeDeploy supports two deployment types for EC2: in-place, which updates the application on existing instances one batch at a time and briefly takes them out of service, and blue/green, which provisions an entirely new fleet, installs the new revision, validates it, and shifts traffic away from the old fleet before terminating it. In-place is simpler and needs no double capacity, but rollback means redeploying the old revision. Blue/green costs more temporarily since two environments coexist, but rollback is nearly instantaneous because the original fleet is untouched until traffic has fully moved; the exam frequently frames 'near-zero-risk rollback' as the tell for blue/green.

concepts.heading: AppSpec Lifecycle Hooks
concepts.body: Every CodeDeploy deployment reads an appspec.yml file that maps application files to destinations and defines lifecycle event hooks such as BeforeInstall, AfterInstall, ApplicationStart, and ValidateService, each of which can run a custom script. These hooks are the mechanism for inserting logic like stopping a service before install or running smoke tests in ValidateService before CodeDeploy considers the deployment successful. If a hook script fails or times out, CodeDeploy marks the deployment failed and can trigger rollback. A common trap: without a real ValidateService check, CodeDeploy only confirms the process started, not that it is actually healthy.

concepts.heading: Lambda Traffic Shifting
concepts.body: For Lambda, CodeDeploy shifts traffic between two function versions using a weighted alias, offering Linear (a fixed percentage shifts at a fixed interval, e.g. 10% every minute), Canary (a small percentage shifts first, then the remainder shifts after a validation window), and All-at-once (immediate full cutover). Both Linear and Canary can pair with CloudWatch alarms so that if error rates breach a threshold during the shift, CodeDeploy automatically halts and rolls back. Choosing Linear versus Canary is mostly about risk tolerance and how much time you want for gradual validation.

concepts.heading: ECS Blue/Green with Task Sets
concepts.body: For ECS services, CodeDeploy performs blue/green by creating a second task set running the new task definition, running health checks and optional validation, then rerouting the load balancer listener to send production traffic to the new task set. The original task set remains running for a configurable wait time, so rollback is simply repointing the listener rather than redeploying containers. This differs from a plain ECS rolling update, which replaces tasks incrementally within the same service without ever standing up a separate, testable environment first.

concepts.heading: Automatic Rollback on Alarm Breach
concepts.body: CodeDeploy deployment groups can be configured to automatically roll back if the deployment itself fails, or if a specified CloudWatch alarm enters ALARM state during a defined monitoring window after traffic shifting begins. This defines success not just as 'the deployment mechanically completed' but as 'metrics stayed within acceptable bounds,' a much stronger safety net than validation scripts alone. Exam scenarios describing 'detect elevated error rates during deployment and revert automatically' point directly at this alarm-triggered rollback feature.

examPoints: When a scenario asks for Lambda traffic to shift gradually in fixed percentage increments over time, the expected answer is a Linear traffic-shifting alias configuration in CodeDeploy, not Canary or All-at-once.

When a scenario requires deployments to automatically revert without human intervention once error rates exceed a threshold, the expected answer is a CodeDeploy deployment group configured with automatic rollback tied to a CloudWatch alarm.

quiz.q: A team deploys a Lambda function and needs traffic to shift to the new version in fixed 10% increments every few minutes, with automatic rollback if error rates spike during the shift. Which CodeDeploy configuration meets this requirement?
choices: A Linear traffic-shifting configuration with a CloudWatch alarm-based rollback
A manually triggered alias update with no monitoring
quiz.explain: Linear configurations shift a fixed percentage of traffic at regular intervals, and pairing it with a CloudWatch alarm enables automatic rollback; All-at-once shifts 100% immediately with no gradual validation window.

quiz.q: An ECS service must be validated on a completely separate set of tasks before any production traffic reaches the new version, with the ability to revert instantly by repointing the load balancer. What should the team use?
choices: ECS blue/green deployment through CodeDeploy with task sets
quiz.explain: ECS blue/green deployments stand up a separate task set that can be validated before the listener is rerouted, unlike a rolling update which replaces tasks within the same live task set.

days.recap: Day 2 covered CodeDeploy's in-place versus blue/green EC2 deployments, how appspec.yml lifecycle hooks insert custom validation, Lambda's Linear/Canary/All-at-once traffic-shifting options, ECS blue/green via task sets, and CloudWatch alarm-triggered automatic rollback.

days.title: Automated Testing Integration: Unit, Integration, and Security Testing

concepts.heading: buildspec.yml Phases
concepts.body: CodeBuild executes a build according to a buildspec.yml file organized into phases: install (set up runtime dependencies), pre_build (e.g. logging into ECR or linting), build (compile and run unit tests), and post_build (package artifacts or push images). Placing test commands inside these phases means CodeBuild treats a non-zero exit code from any command as a phase failure, which fails the build and prevents CodePipeline from advancing. Ordering matters: authentication and dependency installation belong in earlier phases. Forgetting to fail the build on a test failure, such as piping test output to a file without checking the exit code, is a common real-world and exam mistake.

concepts.heading: Quality Gates Across Pipeline Stages
concepts.body: A quality gate is any point in the pipeline where a failure legitimately blocks progress: a unit test failure fails the CodeBuild phase and the build action, while integration tests typically run after a deployment to staging and, if they fail, should stop the pipeline before it reaches production. Structuring the pipeline so failures are caught as early and cheaply as possible (fail fast) reduces the cost of finding defects, so unit tests belong in the build stage and heavier integration tests belong in a dedicated stage after staging, never skipped.

concepts.heading: Security Testing in the Pipeline
concepts.body: Static application security testing (SAST) tools can run as an additional CodeBuild phase to scan source code before an artifact is built into an image. For containerized applications, Amazon ECR image scanning, powered by Amazon Inspector, automatically scans images for known CVEs as soon as they are pushed and continuously rescans them as new vulnerability data is published, without a separate scanning stage. A frequent exam pattern, 'scan container images automatically on every push with no additional pipeline steps,' points directly at enabling ECR scan-on-push rather than a custom Lambda scanner.

concepts.heading: Test Reporting and Visibility
concepts.body: CodeBuild supports test report groups, which parse standard test output formats (JUnit XML, Cucumber JSON) generated during the build and surface pass/fail counts and trends directly in the CodeBuild and CodePipeline consoles. This gives engineers a fast way to see which specific tests failed without digging through raw build logs, and trend data helps identify flaky tests over time. On the exam, 'a team wants to see test failures at a glance in the pipeline console' points to configuring CodeBuild test report groups rather than only relying on CloudWatch Logs.

examPoints: When a requirement states that every image pushed to ECR must be automatically checked for known vulnerabilities without any custom scanning code, the expected answer is enabling ECR image scanning (backed by Amazon Inspector), not a custom Lambda-based scanner.

When a requirement states that a failed unit test must stop the pipeline from proceeding to deployment, the expected answer is relying on the CodeBuild buildspec's phase failure behavior, since a non-zero exit code from the test command fails the build action automatically.

quiz.q: A company wants every container image pushed to Amazon ECR to be automatically scanned for known CVEs without building any custom tooling. What should they configure?
choices: A custom Lambda function triggered on S3 upload
ECR image scanning powered by Amazon Inspector
A manual review process before each push
quiz.explain: ECR image scanning integrates with Amazon Inspector to automatically scan images on push and continuously as new vulnerabilities are discovered, with no custom code required.

quiz.q: A pipeline currently logs test output but does not fail the build when unit tests fail, allowing broken code to reach deployment. What is the most direct fix?
choices: Add a manual approval action after the build stage
Ensure the test command's non-zero exit code propagates so the CodeBuild phase fails
Move testing to a post-deployment step only
quiz.explain: CodeBuild fails a phase when a command returns a non-zero exit code, which stops the pipeline; if output is redirected without checking the exit code, failures can be silently swallowed.

days.recap: Day 3 covered how buildspec.yml phases structure a CodeBuild run, how unit and integration tests act as quality gates, how ECR scan-on-push with Inspector automates container vulnerability detection, and how CodeBuild test report groups surface results.

days.title: Artifact Repositories and Lifecycle Management

concepts.heading: CodeArtifact as a Managed Package Repository
concepts.body: AWS CodeArtifact is a fully managed artifact repository for package formats such as npm, Maven, PyPI, and NuGet, letting an organization host internal packages and control which external packages developers can consume. By configuring an upstream repository pointing to a public registry, CodeArtifact can cache and serve only approved versions, giving security teams a chokepoint to block known-vulnerable packages without developers changing build tooling. This centralization also improves build reliability, since builds pull from a regional AWS endpoint rather than depending on public internet availability.

concepts.heading: ECR Lifecycle Policies
concepts.body: Amazon ECR lifecycle policies are JSON rule sets attached to a repository that automatically expire image tags matching conditions such as 'keep only the most recent 10 tagged images' or 'expire untagged images older than 14 days.' Without lifecycle policies, every pushed image persists indefinitely, driving up storage cost. Rules evaluate in priority order and can target specific tag prefixes, so release-tagged images can be retained far longer than feature-branch build images. 'Automatically clean up old container images to control storage cost' maps directly to an ECR lifecycle policy rather than manual deletion scripts.

concepts.heading: Pipeline Artifact Storage in S3
concepts.body: By default, CodePipeline stores artifacts passed between stages in an S3 bucket, with each stage's output becoming versioned objects that downstream stages consume as inputs. This bucket can be encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key for stronger control over decryption, especially important in cross-account pipelines. S3 versioning also gives an audit trail of exactly which build produced which deployed artifact. A common nuance: if a custom KMS key is used, the pipeline's service role and any cross-account consumer roles need explicit key usage permissions or the pipeline fails at the decrypt step.

concepts.heading: Tag Immutability and Reproducibility
concepts.body: ECR supports tag immutability, which, once enabled, prevents an image tag such as 'prod' from being overwritten by a subsequent push using the same tag; any attempt to reuse a tag is rejected. This guarantees a given tag always refers to exactly the artifact originally built and tested, critical for deployment traceability and reliable rollback. Without immutability, a compromised or careless push could silently replace a production tag with different content. Scenarios describing 'the same tag must always mean the same image' point to enabling tag immutability.

examPoints: When a scenario requires that only approved versions of open-source packages be available to internal developers, the expected answer is AWS CodeArtifact with an upstream repository connected to the public registry, not individual per-project package mirrors.

When a scenario asks for automatic cleanup of old, unused container image tags to reduce storage cost, the expected answer is an ECR lifecycle policy, not a scheduled Lambda function that manually deletes images.

quiz.q: A security team wants to ensure developers can only install npm and Maven packages that have been explicitly approved, without changing developer build tooling. What AWS service should they use?
choices: AWS CodeArtifact with an upstream repository configuration
quiz.explain: CodeArtifact lets an organization proxy and cache a public registry through an upstream repository, so only approved packages are served, without requiring changes to npm or Maven client configuration beyond the registry URL.

quiz.q: A company wants ECR to automatically delete old, unused image tags to control storage costs, keeping only the ten most recent tagged images per repository. What should they configure?
choices: An ECR lifecycle policy with a rule limiting the count of tagged images
S3 lifecycle rules on the ECR bucket
quiz.explain: ECR lifecycle policies directly support rules that expire images based on tag count or age; ECR does not expose its underlying storage as an S3 bucket that customers can configure directly.

days.recap: Day 4 covered CodeArtifact as a controlled, upstream-connected package repository, ECR lifecycle policies for automatic image cleanup, S3-backed pipeline artifact storage with KMS encryption, and tag immutability for reproducible, auditable deployments.

days.title: Deploying to Diverse Compute Targets: EC2, Containers, and Serverless

concepts.heading: EC2 Deployments via the CodeDeploy Agent
concepts.body: For EC2 targets, an agent installed on each instance polls CodeDeploy for new deployment instructions and executes the appspec.yml lifecycle hooks locally, so the agent must be installed, running, and able to reach the CodeDeploy endpoint for a deployment to succeed. Deployment groups can be tied directly to an Auto Scaling group, so whenever the group launches a new instance, CodeDeploy automatically installs the currently deployed revision on it. If the agent is missing or blocked by a security group, the deployment fails with an agent-related error, a very common real-world troubleshooting scenario.

concepts.heading: ECS Deployment Options
concepts.body: ECS supports rolling updates natively, where the service scheduler incrementally replaces old tasks based on minimum/maximum healthy percent settings, and it supports blue/green deployments through CodeDeploy integration using a separate task set. EKS, a different orchestrator, is not natively integrated with CodeDeploy and instead typically relies on GitOps tools like Flux or ArgoCD. Recognizing which orchestrator a scenario describes matters, because 'use CodeDeploy for a Kubernetes deployment' is a distractor.

concepts.heading: Serverless IaC with SAM
concepts.body: The AWS Serverless Application Model (SAM) extends CloudFormation with simplified syntax (AWS::Serverless::Function, AWS::Serverless::Api) purpose-built for Lambda, API Gateway, and DynamoDB. The SAM CLI adds tooling including `sam build` to package dependencies, `sam local invoke` to run and debug functions locally before deploying, and `sam deploy`, which packages artifacts and creates a CloudFormation change set. This local testing capability is SAM's biggest practical advantage over hand-written CloudFormation for serverless workloads.

concepts.heading: CDK Constructs and Synthesis
concepts.body: The CDK lets you define infrastructure in a language like TypeScript or Python, organizing resources into reusable Constructs that can encapsulate best-practice patterns and be shared across teams like any code library. `cdk synth` compiles this into a standard CloudFormation template, and `cdk deploy` executes it through CloudFormation, so all of CloudFormation's safety features still apply underneath. CDK's advantage over SAM or raw CloudFormation is expressing loops, conditionals, and abstraction with real programming language features.

examPoints: When a scenario describes an ECS service that must validate a new version on a separate set of tasks before any production traffic reaches it, the expected answer is ECS blue/green deployment through CodeDeploy, and the same mechanism does not apply to EKS.

When a scenario asks for local testing and debugging of Lambda functions before deployment, the expected answer is the SAM CLI's local invoke capability, which CDK and plain CloudFormation do not provide natively.

quiz.q: A team running workloads on EKS wants to use the same CodeDeploy blue/green deployment mechanism they use for their ECS services. What should they be told?
choices: This works out of the box for EKS
CodeDeploy's native blue/green integration supports ECS and EC2/Lambda but not EKS; a GitOps tool like ArgoCD or Flux should be used instead
EKS requires disabling all deployment automation
quiz.explain: CodeDeploy's deployment platforms are EC2/on-premises, Lambda, and ECS; Kubernetes-based EKS deployments typically use GitOps tooling instead.

quiz.q: A developer wants to test a Lambda function locally, including invoking it with sample events, before deploying it to AWS. Which tool provides this capability most directly?
choices: The SAM CLI with `sam local invoke`
quiz.explain: The SAM CLI specifically provides local invocation and debugging of Lambda functions; CDK and CloudFormation deploy to AWS but do not provide an equivalent local runtime.

days.recap: Day 5 covered how the CodeDeploy agent and Auto Scaling integration handle EC2 deployments, ECS rolling versus blue/green deployment options and their absence for EKS, SAM's serverless-focused syntax and local testing tools, and how CDK constructs synthesize down to ordinary CloudFormation.

days.title: Multi-Account and Multi-Region Pipeline Orchestration

concepts.heading: Cross-Account Deployment Architecture
concepts.body: A common enterprise pattern runs the CI/CD pipeline in a dedicated central tooling account, while deploy actions assume cross-account IAM roles in separate development, staging, and production accounts. This keeps blast radius contained: a compromise of the tooling account's pipeline role does not automatically grant standing access to production, because each target account's role can be scoped tightly and requires an explicit trust relationship back to the tooling account, following least privilege. The exam signal for this pattern is any requirement to deploy centrally while keeping account boundaries and isolation intact.

concepts.heading: Sharing Encrypted Artifacts Across Accounts
concepts.body: Because pipeline artifacts often live in a KMS-encrypted S3 bucket, cross-account deployment requires two layers of permission: an S3 bucket policy granting the target account's role read access, and a KMS key policy explicitly granting that role permission to use the key for decryption. Without the KMS key policy update, the target account can see the object exists but cannot decrypt it, an access-denied error that looks like a permissions problem but is actually a key policy gap. This two-layer requirement is one of the most commonly tested cross-account failure scenarios.

concepts.heading: Multi-Region Deployment Actions
concepts.body: CodePipeline can deploy to regions other than the one hosting the pipeline itself, but each target region needs its own regional artifact bucket, since S3 and KMS resources are regional and cannot be referenced across regions directly. Deployments to multiple regions can run in parallel within a single stage or be sequenced across stages, depending on whether the team wants simultaneous global rollout or a staged canary-by-region approach, typically driven by low-latency global availability or regional disaster recovery needs.

concepts.heading: Pipeline-of-Pipelines
concepts.body: As an organization grows, it often becomes impractical to manage all deployments through one monolithic pipeline; teams instead separate a foundational infrastructure pipeline (provisioning networking and shared services) from application deployment pipelines that consume that shared infrastructure as an input. This separation reduces blast radius and allows infrastructure and application teams to iterate on independent release cadences, typically coordinated through EventBridge or CloudFormation exports/SSM Parameter Store.

examPoints: When a scenario describes a central tooling account deploying to production while preserving strict account isolation, the expected answer is cross-account IAM roles assumed by the pipeline's deploy actions, not a shared credential or a single consolidated account.

When a cross-account deployment fails to access encrypted pipeline artifacts even though the S3 bucket policy already grants access, the expected answer is that the KMS key policy also needs an explicit grant for the target account's role, since S3 access alone does not grant decrypt permission.

quiz.q: A DevOps engineer configures a CodePipeline in a central tooling account to deploy to a production account. The target account's role can read the artifact object in S3 but deployment still fails with a decryption error. What is most likely missing?
choices: A KMS key policy grant allowing the target account's role to use the key
quiz.explain: S3 access alone does not grant permission to decrypt objects encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key; the key policy must separately grant the cross-account role decrypt permission.

quiz.q: An organization wants to deploy the same application to us-east-1 and eu-west-1 simultaneously from a single pipeline defined in us-east-1. What must be true for this to work?
choices: A single shared artifact bucket can serve both regions
Each target region needs its own regional artifact bucket since S3 and KMS resources are regional
Multi-region deployment is not supported by CodePipeline
The pipeline must be duplicated manually in each region
quiz.explain: CodePipeline supports deploying to multiple regions from one pipeline, but each region requires its own artifact bucket because S3 buckets and KMS keys do not span regions.

days.recap: Day 6 covered cross-account pipeline deployment using assumed IAM roles, the two-layer S3-plus-KMS permission model required for cross-account encrypted artifacts, multi-region deployment actions with per-region artifact buckets, and separating infrastructure pipelines from application pipelines.

days.title: Domain 1 Review: SDLC Automation

concepts.heading: Pipeline Anatomy Recap
concepts.body: Domain 1 begins with the core CI/CD pipeline anatomy: a source trigger starts CodePipeline, which orchestrates sequential stages composed of parallel actions, using CodeBuild to compile and test and CodeDeploy to release. Manual Approval actions insert human gates between stages, and event-based triggers keep the loop from commit to build as tight as possible. Trunk-based development, with short-lived branches merged frequently, is the branching model that best supports this level of automation, in contrast to long-lived GitFlow branches.

concepts.heading: Deployment Strategy Selection
concepts.body: Across EC2, Lambda, and ECS, CodeDeploy offers strategies from simple in-place or All-at-once cutovers to gradual Linear and Canary traffic shifting for Lambda, and fully isolated blue/green environments for EC2 and ECS. The unifying theme is a tradeoff between deployment speed, resource cost, and rollback safety: blue/green and gradual shifting cost more or take longer but make rollback nearly instantaneous, while All-at-once is fast but riskier. Automatic rollback tied to CloudWatch alarms is the safety net across all of these strategies.

concepts.heading: Testing and Security as Pipeline Gates
concepts.body: A well-designed pipeline treats every quality and security check as a gate: CodeBuild buildspec phases fail the build on failing unit tests, ECR image scanning through Inspector automatically catches known vulnerabilities on every push, and test report groups make failures visible without digging through raw logs. The exam consistently rewards recognizing which specific AWS-native feature already does this automatically over inventing a custom Lambda-based solution.

concepts.heading: Artifact Governance
concepts.body: CodeArtifact, ECR lifecycle policies, and S3-backed pipeline artifacts together form the artifact governance layer: CodeArtifact controls which open-source packages are consumable, ECR lifecycle policies and tag immutability control container image lifecycle and integrity, and encrypted, versioned S3 artifact buckets preserve a traceable history. Cross-account pipelines add a second dimension, requiring both S3 bucket policies and KMS key policies to safely share encrypted artifacts across account boundaries.

examPoints: Domain 1 exam questions frequently hinge on first identifying the deployment target (EC2, container, or Lambda) and the required traffic-shifting behavior (immediate, gradual, or gated by manual approval) before selecting the correct CodeDeploy configuration.

A second recurring pattern is distinguishing native AWS automation (ECR scanning, buildspec phase failures, lifecycle policies) from unnecessary custom solutions; if AWS already automates something natively, that native feature is almost always the intended answer.

quiz.q: A team needs Lambda traffic to shift gradually with automatic rollback on error spikes, while an ECS team wants to validate a new version on a completely separate environment before any traffic switches. Which two features respectively satisfy these requirements?
choices: Linear or Canary traffic shifting with a CloudWatch alarm; ECS blue/green deployment via CodeDeploy
In-place deployment; Lambda alias without shifting
Manual approval only; CodeBuild test gate only
quiz.explain: Linear/Canary with an alarm-triggered rollback satisfies gradual, safety-netted Lambda deployment, while ECS blue/green via CodeDeploy stands up an isolated task set for pre-traffic validation.

quiz.q: Which AWS-native feature automatically scans container images for known vulnerabilities every time they are pushed to a repository, without custom tooling?
choices: ECR image scanning integrated with Amazon Inspector
quiz.explain: ECR scan-on-push, backed by Amazon Inspector, automatically scans every pushed image; the other options address testing visibility, package governance, or human approval, not vulnerability scanning.

days.recap: Domain 1 review ties together pipeline anatomy, the spectrum of deployment strategies and their rollback tradeoffs, testing and security as automated pipeline gates, and artifact governance across CodeArtifact, ECR, and S3, including the cross-account and multi-region variations.

days.title: Infrastructure as Code Tools: CloudFormation, SAM, and CDK

concepts.heading: CloudFormation Fundamentals
concepts.body: CloudFormation lets you declare AWS resources in YAML or JSON templates, using Parameters for runtime inputs, Conditions to control whether resources are created, and Mappings for static lookup tables, with Macros and custom resources (backed by Lambda) available when built-in intrinsic functions are not expressive enough. Every update to a stack can first be previewed as a Change Set, which shows exactly which resources will be added, modified, or replaced before anything actually changes, letting you catch a destructive replacement, like a database being recreated, before it happens.

concepts.heading: SAM for Serverless
concepts.body: AWS SAM extends CloudFormation with simplified resource types purpose-built for serverless applications, and its CLI tooling (`sam build`, `sam local invoke`, `sam deploy`) adds local testing and streamlined packaging that plain CloudFormation does not offer. Because SAM templates transform into standard CloudFormation templates at deploy time, all CloudFormation deployment mechanics, including change sets and rollback, still apply. SAM is the natural choice when a workload is primarily Lambda, API Gateway, and DynamoDB and the team wants concise syntax plus local debugging.

concepts.heading: CDK and Constructs
concepts.body: The CDK lets teams define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, or other supported languages, organizing resources into Constructs, reusable classes that can bundle several related resources into one importable unit that can be versioned and shared like any other code library. Running `cdk synth` compiles this code into an ordinary CloudFormation template, and `cdk deploy` executes it through CloudFormation, so CDK is best understood as a code-generation layer on top of CloudFormation rather than a separate deployment engine.

concepts.heading: Choosing the Right IaC Tool
concepts.body: The three tools solve overlapping but distinct problems: CloudFormation is the safest choice for teams wanting a single declarative standard everyone can read, SAM is the fastest path for serverless-first teams wanting local testing, and CDK is the best fit when infrastructure patterns need to be abstracted and reused programmatically across many stacks. On the exam, look for the specific pain point named in the scenario, such as 'developers keep copy-pasting similar CloudFormation blocks,' which signals CDK constructs as the answer.

examPoints: When a scenario asks how to preview the exact impact of a stack update before applying it, especially to catch a potentially destructive resource replacement, the expected answer is a CloudFormation change set.

When a scenario describes repeated, boilerplate infrastructure patterns that teams keep copying between templates, the expected answer is abstracting them into reusable AWS CDK constructs rather than continuing to duplicate CloudFormation YAML.

quiz.q: A team wants to know exactly what will happen to their resources, including any that would be destroyed and recreated, before applying a CloudFormation stack update. What should they use?
quiz.explain: A change set previews the specific additions, modifications, and replacements a stack update would make; drift detection instead compares current resource state to the template after the fact.

quiz.q: Multiple teams keep copy-pasting the same CloudFormation resource blocks for a Lambda function, its log group, and its IAM role. What is the best long-term fix?
choices: Keep copying the blocks but add comments
Package the pattern as a reusable AWS CDK construct
Use CloudFormation Macros for every resource
quiz.explain: CDK constructs are designed exactly for encapsulating and reusing common infrastructure patterns as shareable code, reducing duplication far more effectively than copy-pasted templates.

days.recap: Day 8 covered CloudFormation's declarative templates and change sets, SAM's serverless-focused syntax and local testing tools, CDK's programmatic constructs that synthesize into CloudFormation, and how to choose between the three based on team needs.

days.title: Account Provisioning Automation: Organizations, Control Tower, and StackSets

concepts.heading: Control Tower Account Factory
concepts.body: AWS Control Tower's Account Factory automates the creation of new AWS accounts with a consistent baseline already applied, including preventive and detective guardrails, standardized networking, and centralized logging, removing the need to manually configure each new account. Account Factory Customization (AFC) extends this by letting you attach a CloudFormation template to the account provisioning process itself, so custom resources beyond the Control Tower baseline are deployed automatically the moment a new account is created.

concepts.heading: StackSets for Multi-Account, Multi-Region Deployment
concepts.body: CloudFormation StackSets let you define a single template and deploy, update, or delete corresponding stacks across many accounts and regions from one operation, essential once an organization has more than a handful of accounts. StackSets can operate in self-managed mode, requiring manually configured IAM roles, or service-managed mode, which integrates directly with AWS Organizations; service-managed StackSets are almost always preferred at scale because they eliminate manual per-account role setup.

concepts.heading: Service-Managed Permissions and OU Targeting
concepts.body: When a StackSet uses service-managed permissions, it can target an entire Organizational Unit (OU) rather than a fixed list of account IDs, and critically, it automatically deploys the stack to any new account that later joins that OU, with no manual re-run needed. This is the mechanism that keeps baseline resources like standard IAM roles or centralized logging consistently applied as an organization grows, since every new account inherits the OU's StackSet deployments automatically.

concepts.heading: Lifecycle Events for Additional Automation
concepts.body: Control Tower emits lifecycle events, such as CreateManagedAccount, through EventBridge whenever an account is provisioned, enrolled, or updated, and these events can trigger a Lambda function to perform automation beyond what Account Factory or StackSets natively cover, such as registering the new account in an external CMDB or notifying a Slack channel. This event-driven extensibility is how organizations bolt on custom account automation without modifying Control Tower itself.

examPoints: When a scenario requires that every new account automatically receive standard IAM roles and logging configuration the moment it joins a specific OU, the expected answer is a service-managed CloudFormation StackSet targeting that OU, integrated with AWS Organizations.

When a scenario requires custom automation, such as an external system update, to run automatically whenever a new account is provisioned, the expected answer is subscribing to Control Tower lifecycle events through EventBridge and triggering a Lambda function.

quiz.q: A company wants every new AWS account added to its 'Workloads' OU to automatically receive a standard set of IAM roles and CloudTrail configuration with zero manual steps. What should they configure?
choices: A self-managed StackSet with manually created roles in each account
A service-managed StackSet targeting the Workloads OU, integrated with Organizations
A CloudFormation template deployed manually to each account
An SCP that blocks account creation
quiz.explain: Service-managed StackSets integrate with Organizations and automatically deploy to new accounts as they join a targeted OU, requiring no manual role setup or re-deployment.

quiz.q: An organization wants to automatically register newly provisioned AWS accounts in an external inventory system the moment Control Tower finishes creating them. What should they use?
choices: A manually run script after each account creation
Control Tower lifecycle events delivered through EventBridge, triggering a Lambda function
quiz.explain: Control Tower emits lifecycle events (like CreateManagedAccount) to EventBridge that can trigger custom Lambda automation immediately after account provisioning.

days.recap: Day 9 covered how Control Tower Account Factory and its customization feature standardize new account creation, how service-managed StackSets automatically deploy baselines to entire OUs including future accounts, and how lifecycle events enable custom automation on account provisioning.

days.title: Configuration Management: Systems Manager State Manager and AppConfig

concepts.heading: State Manager for Continuous Configuration Enforcement
concepts.body: Systems Manager State Manager lets you define an Association between a document, describing a desired state such as a specific software version, and a set of managed instances, and then continuously or on a schedule reapplies that state so instances that drift back into compliance automatically, without a human running a script. This differs fundamentally from a one-time configuration script because State Manager keeps enforcing the desired state indefinitely, catching manual changes or drift introduced after the fact.

concepts.heading: AppConfig for Dynamic Application Configuration
concepts.body: AWS AppConfig separates application configuration and feature flags from code, letting you change behavior without a code deployment, and critically, it supports deployment strategies (linear or canary rollout of a configuration change) combined with CloudWatch alarm monitoring, so a bad configuration change is automatically rolled back just like a bad code deployment would be. This makes configuration changes as safe as code deployments rather than an unmonitored, all-at-once toggle.

concepts.heading: Validating Configuration Before Deployment
concepts.body: AppConfig supports validators, either a JSON Schema or a Lambda function, that check a proposed configuration value for correctness before it is ever deployed to any host, catching problems like malformed JSON or an out-of-range value before they reach production. This pre-deployment check, combined with gradual deployment strategies and alarm-based rollback, gives AppConfig a full safety pipeline comparable to a code CI/CD pipeline, but for configuration data.

concepts.heading: Managing Configuration Drift
concepts.body: Configuration drift occurs when an instance's actual state diverges from its intended baseline, whether from a manual emergency fix or an incomplete automation run, and State Manager Associations are the primary tool for both detecting and automatically correcting this drift by reapplying the desired-state document on its schedule. Left unmanaged, drift undermines compliance posture and makes incident response harder because no two 'identical' servers are actually identical.

examPoints: When a scenario requires changing a feature flag or application setting safely, gradually, with automatic rollback if metrics degrade, and without redeploying code, the expected answer is AWS AppConfig with a deployment strategy and CloudWatch alarm integration.

When a scenario requires EC2 or on-premises instances to continuously maintain a defined software or configuration baseline, automatically correcting drift, the expected answer is a Systems Manager State Manager Association.

quiz.q: A product team wants to toggle a feature flag for a fraction of users, gradually increase the rollout, and automatically revert if error rates spike, all without redeploying application code. What AWS service fits this requirement?
choices: AWS AppConfig with a deployment strategy and CloudWatch alarm
quiz.explain: AppConfig is purpose-built for dynamic configuration and feature flags with gradual rollout and alarm-triggered rollback; State Manager instead enforces a static desired state on instances, not application-level feature toggles.

quiz.q: A fleet of EC2 instances keeps drifting from its required software configuration due to manual emergency changes. What should be implemented to continuously detect and correct this?
choices: A one-time Systems Manager Run Command
A Systems Manager State Manager Association applied on a recurring schedule
quiz.explain: State Manager Associations continuously (or on a schedule) reapply the desired configuration document, correcting drift automatically, unlike a one-time Run Command execution.

days.recap: Day 10 covered how State Manager Associations continuously enforce and correct configuration drift on instances, how AppConfig safely deploys dynamic application settings and feature flags with gradual rollout and alarm-based rollback, and how validators catch bad configuration before deployment.

days.title: Patch and Inventory Automation

concepts.heading: Patch Baselines and Patch Groups
concepts.body: Systems Manager Patch Manager uses a patch baseline to define which patches are automatically approved, for example only security patches classified as Critical or Important after an approval delay of a set number of days, and patch groups, which are tags used to segment instances so that production and development can follow different baselines with different approval rules and timing. This separation lets a team apply looser, faster patching to development while keeping stricter controls for production.

concepts.heading: Maintenance Windows
concepts.body: A Maintenance Window schedules when patching, or any other Systems Manager task, is allowed to run, letting an organization confine potentially disruptive activity like a patch-induced reboot to low-traffic hours and avoid patching during business-critical periods. Maintenance Windows also support setting a maximum concurrency and a maximum error threshold, so if too many targets fail during a patch run, the window stops executing further targets rather than potentially taking down an entire fleet at once.

concepts.heading: Inventory for Fleet Visibility
concepts.body: Systems Manager Inventory automatically collects and centralizes metadata from managed instances, including installed applications, files, and network configuration, giving a single place to answer questions like 'which instances still have an outdated version of this library installed' without manually logging into each host. This data feeds directly into vulnerability response and into compliance audits that require proof of what software is actually running.

concepts.heading: Patch Compliance Reporting
concepts.body: Patch Manager produces compliance reports showing which instances are fully patched, missing patches, or failed a patch operation, and this compliance data can be combined with AWS Config rules to automatically flag or even trigger remediation on non-compliant instances. This closes the loop from defining a patch policy to verifying, at scale, that the policy is actually being followed.

examPoints: When a scenario requires that only approved security patches be applied to production instances during a specific low-traffic time window, the expected answer is combining a Patch Manager patch baseline and patch group with a Maintenance Window, not a manually scheduled script.
When a scenario requires centrally knowing what software is installed across hundreds of instances without manually checking each one, the expected answer is Systems Manager Inventory.

quiz.q: A company wants only approved security patches applied to production EC2 instances, and only during a scheduled weekend maintenance period. Which combination of Systems Manager features achieves this?
choices: A patch baseline and patch group combined with a Maintenance Window
quiz.explain: A patch baseline defines which patches are approved, a patch group segments which instances that baseline applies to, and a Maintenance Window restricts when the patching operation is allowed to run.

quiz.q: A security team needs to quickly determine which of thousands of EC2 instances have a specific outdated library installed, in response to a newly disclosed vulnerability. What should they use?
quiz.explain: Systems Manager Inventory centrally collects installed software details from managed instances, allowing a fast, fleet-wide query rather than manual per-instance inspection.

days.recap: Day 11 covered how Patch Manager's baselines and patch groups control which patches apply where, how Maintenance Windows schedule and limit the blast radius of patch operations, how Inventory gives fleet-wide software visibility, and how compliance reporting closes the loop with Config Rules.

days.title: Compliance Automation: Config Rules and Auto-Remediation

concepts.heading: Config Rules for Continuous Evaluation
concepts.body: AWS Config continuously evaluates whether your resource configurations comply with rules you define, either using AWS managed rules covering common best practices or custom rules backed by a Lambda function, and it flags any non-compliant resource with a NON_COMPLIANT status visible in the console and queryable through the API. This continuous evaluation distinguishes Config from a one-time audit; new resources and configuration changes are evaluated automatically going forward.

concepts.heading: Automated Remediation
concepts.body: Config Remediation attaches a Systems Manager Automation document to a rule so that, when a resource is found non-compliant, AWS can automatically execute a corrective action, for example automatically blocking public access on an S3 bucket the moment it is detected as publicly exposed, with no human intervention required. Remediation can trigger automatically on every non-compliance detection or require manual execution, and it supports retry attempts and a maximum automatic remediation count to avoid remediation loops.

concepts.heading: Conformance Packs for Framework-Level Compliance
concepts.body: A Conformance Pack bundles a set of Config rules and their associated remediation actions into a single deployable template that maps to a specific compliance framework such as PCI-DSS or HIPAA, letting an organization deploy dozens of related rules consistently rather than configuring each rule by hand in every account. Conformance Packs can be deployed organization-wide, ensuring every account inherits the same rule set and stays aligned even as new accounts are added.

concepts.heading: Aggregating Compliance Across the Organization
concepts.body: A Config Aggregator collects configuration and compliance data from multiple accounts and regions into a single account, giving a security or compliance team one place to see the overall compliance posture of the entire organization rather than logging into each account individually. This is essential at scale, since a per-account view does not answer 'how many S3 buckets across the whole company are publicly accessible right now,' a question aggregation is specifically designed to answer quickly.

examPoints: When a scenario requires that a publicly exposed S3 bucket be automatically locked down the instant it is detected, with no human in the loop, the expected answer is an AWS Config rule paired with Config Remediation using a Systems Manager Automation document.

When a scenario requires deploying the same PCI-DSS-aligned set of compliance rules consistently across every account in an organization, the expected answer is a Conformance Pack, not individually configured Config rules per account.

quiz.q: A security team wants any S3 bucket that becomes publicly accessible to have that access automatically removed within minutes, without anyone manually intervening. What should they configure?
choices: A Config rule alone, with manual review
A Config rule combined with automatic remediation using a Systems Manager Automation document
Alert notifications only, with no action
A Conformance Pack with no remediation action
quiz.explain: Config Remediation is what actually executes a corrective action automatically when a rule detects non-compliance; the rule alone only detects and reports.

quiz.q: An organization with 40 AWS accounts wants to deploy the same set of PCI-DSS-related Config rules consistently to every account, including future ones. What is the most efficient approach?
choices: Manually configure the rules in each account
quiz.explain: Conformance Packs bundle related rules into one deployable unit that can be applied consistently across an organization, avoiding manual per-account configuration. CloudTrail Lake does not deploy rules (and has been closed to new customers since 2026-05-31).

days.recap: Day 12 covered how Config rules continuously evaluate compliance, how Remediation automatically corrects non-compliant resources using Systems Manager Automation, how Conformance Packs bundle rules into deployable compliance frameworks, and how a Config Aggregator centralizes compliance visibility across accounts.

days.title: Domain 2 Review: Configuration Management and IaC

concepts.heading: IaC as the Foundation
concepts.body: Domain 2 builds outward from Day 8's IaC tools: CloudFormation's change sets, SAM's serverless focus with local testing, and CDK's programmatic constructs all serve as the mechanism by which every other automation in this domain, account baselines, patch policies, and compliance remediation, actually gets deployed and kept consistent. Every subsequent topic in the domain assumes resources are defined as code rather than clicked together manually.

concepts.heading: Provisioning Consistency at Scale
concepts.body: Control Tower Account Factory and service-managed StackSets solve the problem of keeping every account, present and future, aligned to the same baseline automatically, while lifecycle events allow custom automation to hook into the account provisioning process itself. The unifying idea is that manual, per-account setup does not scale and must be replaced by OU-level, event-driven automation.

concepts.heading: Keeping Running Systems in Their Intended State
concepts.body: State Manager and AppConfig both address configuration drift, but at different layers: State Manager keeps instance-level software and configuration state aligned to a defined baseline, while AppConfig manages application-level settings and feature flags with gradual, monitored rollout. Patch Manager and Inventory extend this same idea specifically to security patching and fleet-wide software visibility, ensuring that both the operating system layer and the application layer stay in a known, verifiable state rather than silently drifting apart from one another over time.

concepts.heading: Compliance as Continuous Automation
concepts.body: AWS Config rules, automated remediation, and Conformance Packs turn compliance from a periodic manual audit into a continuously enforced, self-healing system, and Config Aggregators extend that visibility across an entire multi-account organization. The consistent exam theme across all of Domain 2 is recognizing which Systems Manager or Config capability automatically detects and corrects a specific kind of drift or violation.

examPoints: Domain 2 exam questions often hinge on precisely distinguishing similarly named Systems Manager capabilities: State Manager enforces general configuration state, Patch Manager specifically handles patching, and Inventory only collects information without enforcing anything.

A second recurring pattern is distinguishing detection-only tools (a Config rule by itself) from detection-plus-correction tools (a Config rule with Remediation attached); read scenarios carefully for whether automatic correction, not just alerting, is required.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes Systems Manager State Manager from Patch Manager?
choices: They are interchangeable names for the same feature
State Manager continuously enforces a general desired configuration state, while Patch Manager specifically manages patch baselines, groups, and patch compliance
Patch Manager only collects inventory data
State Manager only applies to Windows instances
quiz.explain: State Manager is a general-purpose desired-state enforcement tool via Associations, while Patch Manager is specialized for patch baselines, patch groups, and patch compliance reporting.

quiz.q: A Config rule detects a non-compliant resource but nothing happens to fix it automatically. What is missing?
choices: A Remediation action (Systems Manager Automation document) attached to the rule
quiz.explain: A Config rule alone only detects and reports non-compliance; automatic correction requires an attached Remediation configuration using a Systems Manager Automation document.

days.recap: Domain 2 review connects IaC tooling as the deployment foundation, automated account provisioning at scale via Control Tower and StackSets, continuous configuration and patch enforcement via State Manager and Patch Manager, and compliance automation via Config Rules, Remediation, and Conformance Packs.

days.title: Designing Multi-AZ and Multi-Region High Availability

concepts.heading: Multi-AZ Deployment as the HA Baseline
concepts.body: Spreading resources across at least two Availability Zones is the baseline requirement for high availability on AWS, since each AZ is a physically separate facility with independent power, cooling, and networking, so a failure in one AZ should not take down the whole application. An Application or Network Load Balancer automatically distributes traffic across healthy targets in multiple AZs and stops routing to any target that fails its health checks, without any manual intervention needed to detect and route around a failure.

concepts.heading: RDS Multi-AZ Failover Mechanics
concepts.body: RDS Multi-AZ maintains a synchronously replicated standby instance in a different AZ from the primary, and when the primary fails or undergoes maintenance, RDS automatically promotes the standby and repoints the same DNS endpoint to it, meaning the application's connection string never needs to change. This synchronous replication also improves durability, not just availability, because a committed write exists on both the primary and standby before being acknowledged. A common exam trap confuses Multi-AZ with read replicas, which use a separate endpoint and asynchronous replication for read scaling, not automatic failover.

concepts.heading: Multi-Region Availability Patterns
concepts.body: For availability requirements beyond a single region, Route 53 failover or weighted routing directs traffic away from an unhealthy region, but the application data layer must also be replicated across regions to make this meaningful, using services like Aurora Global Database or DynamoDB Global Tables. Without cross-region data replication, a Route 53 failover to another region only redirects traffic to a region with no usable data, so DNS-level failover and data-layer replication must always be designed together.

concepts.heading: Availability Math for Serial and Parallel Components
concepts.body: When an architecture chains components together serially, the overall availability is the product of each component's individual availability, meaning even components that are each 99.9% available combine to a lower overall figure, and this compounding effect is often underestimated. Introducing redundancy so critical components are available in parallel raises the effective availability of that layer, and is the standard technique for correcting an architecture whose calculated end-to-end availability falls short of its target SLA.

examPoints: When a scenario requires that an RDS primary failure be handled automatically with no change to the application's connection string, the expected answer is RDS Multi-AZ, not a read replica, which uses a separate endpoint and asynchronous replication.

When a scenario describes an architecture whose overall calculated availability is lower than expected because several components are chained serially, the expected answer is introducing parallel redundancy at the weakest serial components, not simply adding more serial steps.

quiz.q: An application must continue operating without any connection string change if its RDS primary database instance fails unexpectedly. Which RDS feature satisfies this requirement?
choices: A read replica in another AZ
A single-AZ deployment with automated backups
quiz.explain: RDS Multi-AZ automatically fails over to a synchronously replicated standby and keeps the same DNS endpoint; read replicas use a separate endpoint and are designed for read scaling, not automatic failover.

quiz.q: An architecture chains four components serially, each individually available 99.95% of the time, resulting in an overall availability below the required SLA. What is the most effective fix?
choices: Add more serial components for redundancy
Introduce parallel redundancy for the weakest components in the chain
quiz.explain: Serial components multiply their availability figures together, lowering the total; parallel redundancy at key components raises the effective availability of that layer and improves the overall calculation.

days.recap: Day 14 covered multi-AZ deployment as the HA baseline, RDS Multi-AZ's synchronous replication and same-endpoint automatic failover, multi-region patterns combining Route 53 with Aurora Global Database or DynamoDB Global Tables, and the math showing why serial components need parallel redundancy to meet availability targets.

days.title: Scalable Architectures: Auto Scaling and Distributed Design

concepts.heading: EC2 Auto Scaling Policy Types
concepts.body: EC2 Auto Scaling supports target tracking, automatically adjusting capacity to keep a chosen metric at a target value without manually defining thresholds; step scaling, defining different scaling adjustments for different breach magnitudes; and simple scaling, a single adjustment per alarm, now largely superseded by the other two. Target tracking is the recommended default for most workloads because it requires the least tuning and adapts automatically as load patterns change.

concepts.heading: Decoupling for Independent Scalability
concepts.body: Replacing synchronous, direct calls between components with asynchronous messaging through SQS, SNS, or EventBridge allows each component to scale independently based on its own load, so a slow or overloaded downstream service does not directly block or crash the upstream caller. A producer can keep accepting work even if a consumer is temporarily backed up, because the queue absorbs the burst rather than propagating backpressure directly to the caller.

concepts.heading: Scaling Workers Based on Queue Depth
concepts.body: A very common pattern scales a fleet of worker instances based on an SQS queue depth metric, typically ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible, using a target tracking policy that aims to keep messages per worker at a target ratio, so the fleet automatically grows when the queue backs up and shrinks when it drains. This ties compute capacity directly to actual work waiting to be done, a more accurate scaling signal for queue-driven workloads than a generic CPU-based policy.

concepts.heading: Serverless Concurrency Controls
concepts.body: Lambda scales concurrency automatically and near-instantly in response to incoming request volume, but Reserved Concurrency caps the maximum number of concurrent executions a function can use, protecting downstream systems or other functions sharing the account's concurrency pool, while Provisioned Concurrency keeps a specified number of execution environments pre-initialized and warm, eliminating cold-start latency at the cost of paying for that capacity continuously. Choosing between them depends on whether the goal is limiting maximum usage or guaranteeing consistent low latency.

examPoints: When a scenario requires worker EC2 instance count to scale directly in proportion to the number of messages waiting in an SQS queue, the expected answer is a target tracking Auto Scaling policy based on queue depth, such as ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible.

When a scenario requires eliminating Lambda cold-start latency for a consistently invoked, latency-sensitive function, the expected answer is Provisioned Concurrency, not Reserved Concurrency, which only caps maximum usage rather than pre-warming environments.

quiz.q: A team runs a fleet of EC2 workers that process messages from an SQS queue and wants the fleet size to automatically track the backlog of unprocessed messages. What should they configure?
choices: A target tracking scaling policy based on SQS queue depth
Simple scaling based on CPU only
quiz.explain: Queue-depth-based target tracking ties worker capacity directly to the actual backlog of work, which is a more accurate signal than a generic CPU metric for queue-driven workloads.

quiz.q: A latency-sensitive Lambda function suffers noticeable delay on its first invocation after periods of inactivity. Which setting most directly resolves this?
quiz.explain: Provisioned Concurrency keeps execution environments pre-initialized and warm, directly eliminating cold-start latency, whereas Reserved Concurrency only caps maximum concurrent executions.

days.recap: Day 15 covered Auto Scaling's target tracking, step, and simple scaling policies, how decoupling with SQS/SNS/EventBridge lets components scale independently, queue-depth-based worker scaling, and the distinction between Lambda's Reserved and Provisioned Concurrency.

days.title: Disaster Recovery Strategies: RTO/RPO-Driven Design

concepts.heading: The Four DR Strategies Through a DevOps Lens
concepts.body: The four standard DR strategies, backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, and multi-site active-active, form a spectrum of increasing cost and decreasing RTO/RPO, but the real DevOps differentiator is how much of the recovery is automated through IaC versus manual: backup and restore typically involves manually restoring infrastructure from scratch, while pilot light and warm standby rely on IaC to rapidly scale up pre-defined but minimal infrastructure the moment a disaster is declared.

concepts.heading: Automating the Pilot Light Pattern
concepts.body: In a pilot light setup, only the smallest core infrastructure runs continuously in the DR region, and when a disaster is declared, a CloudFormation or CDK deployment pipeline rapidly provisions the remaining application tier to full production capacity in the DR region. Automating this scale-up step, rather than manually clicking through console screens during an actual outage, is what turns pilot light from a theoretical strategy into a practically achievable RTO.

concepts.heading: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS)
concepts.body: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery continuously replicates block-level changes from source servers to a staging area in a target AWS region, enabling recovery point objectives measured in seconds and recovery time objectives measured in minutes, dramatically faster than backup-and-restore-based approaches. DRS supports non-disruptive recovery drills, launching temporary recovery instances in an isolated test environment to validate that a real failover would actually work, without touching production or the ongoing replication.

concepts.heading: Automating and Testing DR Regularly
concepts.body: A DR plan that has never been tested is not a reliable DR plan, so mature organizations automate DR drills, triggering them on a schedule using Lambda or Step Functions to launch DRS recovery instances or spin up pilot-light infrastructure in an isolated manner, validate the result against expected health checks, and tear it back down. This turns disaster recovery validation into a routine, low-friction, repeatable pipeline step rather than a rare, high-stress, manual fire drill.

examPoints: When a scenario describes keeping only minimal infrastructure running in a secondary region and using IaC to rapidly scale it to full capacity only when a disaster is declared, the expected answer is the pilot light strategy automated with CloudFormation or CDK.

When a scenario requires validating disaster recovery readiness regularly without impacting production or actually failing over, the expected answer is running a non-disruptive DR drill, such as AWS DRS's recovery drill feature launching isolated test instances.

quiz.q: A company wants to keep only a minimal database replica running in a secondary region during normal operations, and use CloudFormation to rapidly provision full application capacity only if a disaster is declared. Which DR strategy does this describe?
choices: Pilot light, automated with IaC-based scale-up
Warm standby with full capacity always running
quiz.explain: Pilot light keeps only minimal core infrastructure running continuously and relies on IaC automation to scale up the rest only when needed, distinguishing it from warm standby which keeps a scaled-down but fully functional copy always running.

quiz.q: A team needs to regularly verify that their disaster recovery failover would actually work, without impacting production systems or ongoing data replication. What should they use?
choices: A manual full failover test in production
AWS DRS's non-disruptive recovery drill launching isolated test instances
Skipping testing and trusting the documented plan
quiz.explain: DRS recovery drills launch temporary, isolated recovery instances specifically to validate failover readiness without disrupting production or the live replication stream.

days.recap: Day 16 covered the four DR strategies viewed through automation maturity, how pilot light relies on IaC to rapidly scale up in a disaster, how AWS DRS achieves seconds-level RPO and minutes-level RTO through continuous block replication, and why regular automated DR drills are essential.

days.title: Resilience Testing and Automatic Recovery

concepts.heading: AWS Fault Injection Simulator Fundamentals
concepts.body: AWS Fault Injection Simulator (FIS) lets you define an Experiment Template describing a controlled fault, such as terminating a random EC2 instance or simulating an AZ network disruption, and run it against real infrastructure to observe how the system actually responds, rather than relying only on theoretical resilience assumptions. Every experiment template can include one or more Stop Conditions, tied to CloudWatch alarms, that automatically halt the experiment the instant real customer impact exceeds an acceptable threshold, which is what makes running fault injection against production responsible rather than reckless.

concepts.heading: Chaos Engineering Principles
concepts.body: Sound chaos engineering starts by defining a hypothesis about steady-state behavior, then runs the smallest possible experiment to test that hypothesis, deliberately minimizing blast radius before gradually expanding scope as confidence grows. This disciplined, incremental approach is what separates chaos engineering from simply breaking things randomly, and it is the reasoning the exam expects when a scenario describes planning a new resilience experiment.

concepts.heading: Native Auto-Recovery Mechanisms
concepts.body: Several AWS services provide automatic recovery without any custom fault-injection tooling: an Application or Network Load Balancer automatically stops routing to targets that fail health checks, an Auto Scaling group automatically terminates and replaces instances that fail their health checks, and EC2 Auto Recovery automatically recovers an instance, preserving its instance ID, IPs, and data, when the underlying hardware experiences a detectable failure. Recognizing these as always-on, built-in mechanisms is important for correctly scoping what FIS experiments actually need to validate.

concepts.heading: Integrating Resilience Testing into CI/CD
concepts.body: Rather than running FIS experiments only occasionally and manually, mature teams schedule them to run automatically as part of a pipeline after each significant deployment, verifying that the new release has not silently degraded the system's ability to tolerate a failure it previously tolerated correctly. This closes the loop between testing resilience once and continuously verifying resilience holds as the system evolves, treating resilience the same way automated tests treat functional correctness.

examPoints: When a scenario requires a chaos experiment to automatically stop before it causes unacceptable real customer impact, the expected answer is configuring a Stop Condition in the FIS experiment template tied to a CloudWatch alarm.

When a scenario asks how to ensure new deployments have not degraded the system's fault tolerance, the expected answer is integrating FIS experiments into the CI/CD pipeline so resilience is verified after every significant release.

quiz.q: A team wants to run a chaos engineering experiment against production but must guarantee it will automatically stop if real customer-facing error rates spike beyond an acceptable level. What FIS feature should they configure?
choices: A Stop Condition tied to a CloudWatch alarm
Running the experiment only in a test account
quiz.explain: A Stop Condition automatically halts an FIS experiment when a linked CloudWatch alarm enters ALARM state, protecting against excessive real-world impact.

quiz.q: A team wants to ensure that every new deployment has not silently reduced the system's ability to tolerate a previously-verified failure scenario. What should they do?
choices: Run a single FIS experiment once, at launch, and never again
Integrate FIS experiments into the CI/CD pipeline to run after significant deployments
Rely only on load balancer health checks
Disable Auto Scaling health checks to simplify testing
quiz.explain: Running FIS experiments automatically as part of the pipeline after deployments continuously verifies that resilience has not regressed, rather than assuming a one-time test remains valid forever.

days.recap: Day 17 covered FIS experiment templates and Stop Conditions for safe chaos engineering, the discipline of hypothesis-driven, blast-radius-limited experimentation, native auto-recovery mechanisms in ELB, Auto Scaling, and EC2, and integrating resilience testing into CI/CD.

days.title: Domain 3 Review: Resilient Cloud Solutions

concepts.heading: High Availability Foundations
concepts.body: Domain 3 begins with the building blocks of availability: spreading resources across AZs, using RDS Multi-AZ for automatic, same-endpoint database failover, and extending availability across regions with Route 53 combined with a cross-region data replication service like Aurora Global Database or DynamoDB Global Tables. The recurring exam theme is recognizing that DNS-level failover alone is meaningless without a correctly replicated data layer behind it.

concepts.heading: Designing for Elastic Scale
concepts.body: Scalability in Domain 3 rests on Auto Scaling policies, especially target tracking, and on decoupling architecture with SQS, SNS, or EventBridge so components can scale independently rather than propagating backpressure directly between tightly coupled services. Queue-depth-based scaling and Lambda's Provisioned versus Reserved Concurrency are the specific mechanisms most often tested, and both illustrate the same underlying principle: capacity should track the actual amount of pending work rather than a generic proxy metric like CPU utilization alone.

concepts.heading: Disaster Recovery as an Automation Problem
concepts.body: The four DR strategies matter less as abstract categories and more as a spectrum of how much recovery is pre-automated with IaC; pilot light and warm standby specifically depend on CloudFormation or CDK to rapidly scale infrastructure during an actual disaster, and AWS DRS provides continuous replication with fast, drill-tested recovery. The consistent theme is that untested DR plans should not be trusted, which is why regular, automated, non-disruptive drills matter.

concepts.heading: Validating Resilience Continuously
concepts.body: FIS experiments, guarded by Stop Conditions, let teams deliberately verify that native auto-recovery mechanisms actually behave as expected under real fault conditions, and integrating these experiments into CI/CD ensures resilience is continuously re-validated as the system changes, rather than assumed to hold indefinitely. This closes the loop between designing for resilience on paper and proving, with evidence from real experiments, that the system actually tolerates the failures it was designed to survive.

examPoints: Domain 3 scenarios often require distinguishing an availability solution (Multi-AZ, ELB, Route 53 failover) from a durability or scaling solution (read replicas, Global Tables, Auto Scaling); read the scenario for whether it is asking about surviving a failure or handling more load.

A second common pattern tests whether a described DR or resilience mechanism is automated (IaC-driven pilot light scale-up, FIS with Stop Conditions) versus manual, since the exam consistently favors automated, tested solutions over manual, ad hoc processes.

quiz.q: Which pairing correctly distinguishes an availability mechanism from a scaling mechanism?
choices: RDS Multi-AZ (availability) and EC2 Auto Scaling target tracking (scaling)
Aurora Global Database (scaling) and Auto Scaling (availability)
quiz.explain: RDS Multi-AZ exists to survive a failure with automatic failover (availability), while Auto Scaling target tracking exists to handle varying load (scaling); these solve different problems even though both improve overall reliability.

quiz.q: A DR strategy keeps minimal infrastructure running and uses CloudFormation to scale up to full capacity only when a disaster is declared. Which strategy and mechanism does this describe?
choices: Multi-site active-active, using DynamoDB Global Tables
Pilot light, automated with IaC-based scale-up
Backup and restore, using manual console steps
Warm standby with full capacity always running
quiz.explain: This is the defining characteristic of pilot light: minimal always-on infrastructure plus IaC automation to rapidly scale up only during an actual disaster.

days.recap: Domain 3 review ties together high availability design across AZs and regions, elastic and decoupled scaling patterns, disaster recovery strategies automated through IaC, and continuous resilience validation through FIS-driven chaos experiments.

days.title: Safe Log and Metric Collection and Storage
